story.title: North Korea’s Deepfake Calls Fueled Over $400M in Crypto Theft, DOJ Says - Bitcoin Foundation

facts.text: State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.

According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.

U.S. authorities identified more than 900 webcam videos that hackers secretly recorded of tech workers, who were deceived in the massive North Korean operation.

An FBI alert earlier this week notes that the North Korean threat actor hijacked accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord, and used them to invite victims to video meetings under various pretenses.

"North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months."
"Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target's trust."
The agency said it's "aware of several other attempts by North Korean hackers to target software developers, maintainers, and software libraries with significant download volume."

In an extensive report shared with The Hacker News in July 2026, JUMPSEC revealed how the social engineering operation is built atop a phishing kit designed to impersonate videoconferencing platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams.

The cybersecurity company has characterized FaceStealer as a victim acquisition platform that involves using compromised trusted contacts as a pathway to fuel a self-propagating attack chain via Telegram.

"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman in a statement.

The US has seized servers linked to a North Korean scam that used fake video meetings and deepfakes to steal more than $400 million in crypto, and has moved to seize $1.2 billion that was taken from Binance.
"North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft," said M.
Scott Proctor, the department's principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security.
North Korea has denied involvement in the Binance hack.
AP put the figure at about $6.3 billion (5.7 billion euros) and called it the biggest crypto heist on record.
The FBI says hackers are also starting to use AI-generated deepfakes of well-known crypto figures.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," said Patrick Grandy, who heads the FBI's Los Angeles field office.
Under a federal warrant, the FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos of victims.
